Here we use sulfur K-edge micro-X-ray absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy to measure the relative abundances of S 6+ , S 4+ and S 2− in apatite inclusions hosted by geochemically characterized and dated zircons from sub-arc sanukitoid magmas that span 3.4 billion years of Earth’s geological history. The sub-arc mantle shows marked increase in oxygen fugacity between 3.4 and 3.0 billion years ago (Ga). It is substantially more oxidized than unaltered ambient upper mantle, a characteristic that cannot be explained by fractionation, degassing or intrinsic mantle processes. We propose that progressive oxidative weathering enhanced the proportion of oxidized sulfur recycled to mantle wedge sources, establishing feedback between subduction of surface materials and incrementally oxidized arc magmatism. Early subduction involving inorganic oxidation and ‘whiffs’ of oxygen between 3.4 and 2.7 Ga may have regulated an early increase in fugacity of the sub-arc mantle before the Great Oxidation Event, matching similar conditions to the modern Earth by 2.1 Ga.

title: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
abstract: Arctic sea ice decline has been observed across all seasons and is projected to continue in the future. Relative to historical observations, climate models show their largest biases and uncertainties during winter, when ice cover strongly regulates air–sea heat exchange, ocean mixing and atmospheric circulation. Palaeoclimate records offer opportunities to evaluate model performance beyond the historical period, but applications have remained largely qualitative. Here we compile an Arctic-wide database of mid-Holocene (5–7 thousand years ago) biomarkers to assess sea ice simulations of this past warm period. Using a recently developed proxy system model, we present a Bayesian palaeoclimate model weighting scheme that refines the multi-model mean winter sea ice extent through fully quantitative proxy-model comparisons, accounting for model interdependence and non-stationary proxy seasonality. We demonstrate that, by adjusting the contribution of each model to the ensemble mean based on proxy evidence, model weights can eliminate biases and reduce uncertainties by 85%, to the level of interannual variability. Weighted projections using the same climate models indicate that future winter sea ice extent may be nearly 1 million km 2 lower than prior estimates across forthcoming decades and possible emissions scenarios, with broad implications for Arctic ecosystems, mid-latitude weather, and cryosphere stability.

title: Trade-offs between soil inorganic and organic carbon driven by multiple global environmental changes
abstract: Dryland ecosystems store large amounts of both soil organic and inorganic carbon, yet the responses of soil inorganic carbon to global environmental change remain largely overlooked despite the potential vulnerability of this carbon pool. Here we aim to determine how soil inorganic and organic carbon respond to multiple global change drivers (warming, reactive nitrogen input and altered precipitation) using an 8-year field manipulation experiment in a semi-arid grassland and a meta-analysis based on 44 observations. We found that altered precipitation has no effect on soil inorganic carbon, but warming and nitrogen input interactively affect it. Specifically, nitrogen input alone does not affect soil inorganic carbon, but it increases soil inorganic carbon loss (~9.1%) when combined with climate warming. This inorganic carbon loss co-occurs with enhanced microbial nitrogen mineralization and nitrification, suggesting that enhancement of proton production due to nitrification controls soil inorganic carbon dissolution and persistence. Furthermore, both the field study and meta-analysis show that nitrogen input and/or warming induce contrasting changes in soil inorganic and organic carbon, suggesting a trade-off between soil inorganic and organic carbon under these two major global change drivers. These results highlight the need to account for the vulnerability of soil inorganic carbon when predicting dryland carbon dynamics under future climate change scenarios.

title: Decolonize soil erosion modelling
abstract: Uncritical extrapolation of soil erosion models developed in the Global North to Global South settings for which they were not designed reflects and perpetuates neocolonial biases in geoscience. To build a more accurate and equitable understanding of land degradation, we must rethink erosion research.

title: Antarctic marine-based ice destabilized when warming outpaces solid-Earth feedbacks
abstract: The Antarctic Ice Sheet is expected to be the largest contributor to sea-level rise over the coming centuries. Previous equilibrium ice-sheet simulations have suggested that this is due to crossing a bifurcation point associated with marine ice-sheet instability. Here we investigate whether sectors vulnerable to this instability can undergo rate-induced tipping, whereby rapid forcing and slow bedrock uplift trigger self-sustained retreat before the bifurcation point is reached. We test this with an ice-sheet model coupled to a glacial isostatic adjustment model, sampling the uncertainty in mantle viscosity. We find that slow bedrock adjustment weakens the stabilizing effect of glacial isostatic adjustment, allowing grounding lines to reach retrograde bed slopes more readily and triggering self-sustained retreat below the bifurcation threshold. Although the West Antarctic Ice Sheet is subject to a bifurcation, it is unlikely to experience rate-induced tipping because of the low mantle viscosity beneath the region. In contrast, the Recovery and Aurora subglacial basins are likely to undergo such a transition even under warming rates lower than those observed today. Depending on mantle viscosity, this mechanism can reduce the critical global mean temperature anomaly by up to 0.5 K, with important implications for the long-term evolution of the Earth system.

title: The Baffin Bay Ice Shelf stabilized three adjacent ice sheets during the last glacial period
abstract: Global ice volume peaked between ~26,500 and 19,000 years ago and resulted in the Laurentide, Innuitian and Greenland ice sheets coalescing in Baffin Bay, a semi-enclosed basin between Greenland and Canada. However, the configuration of their marine terminating margins, which help establish the boundary conditions and sensitivity to processes that govern ice-sheet retreat, remains unclear. Here we compile bathymetric data and report a geomorphic study of the Baffin Bay continental slope. We provide evidence for slope-grounded ice during the last glacial interval and trace its maximum depth imprint around most of Baffin Bay. We interpret ice-contact features to have resulted from a basin-spanning ice shelf that was ~1,400–2,100 m thick, once corrected for relative sea level. The extensive ice shelf (150,000 km 2 ), supported by the basin geometry, buttressed, mechanically coupled, and promoted thickening of the adjacent ice sheets. Informed by sediment cores, we infer that ice-shelf collapse triggered rapid ice-sheet retreat, linking abrupt Northern Hemisphere ice-sheet instability to embayment-scale ice-shelf dynamics. The Baffin Bay Ice Shelf shows that ice-shelf loss can rapidly reorganize marine ice sheets, an analogue for how weakening buttresses may accelerate future Antarctica ice-stream retreat.

title: An Arctic ice shelf in the Last Glacial Maximum rivalled Antarctica’s modern ice shelves
abstract: Ice shelves stabilize marine-terminating ice sheets, and their loss can trigger rapid, irreversible ice-sheet retreat. New geomorphic evidence for a multi-kilometre-thick ice shelf in Baffin Bay during the last glacial period constrains the maximum extents of three surrounding ice sheets and demonstrates that their stability was fundamentally linked.

title: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
abstract: Terrestrial vegetation regulates global carbon cycling and climate through responses to water availability. Yet, it remains unclear whether soil moisture (SM) or atmospheric dryness (vapour pressure deficit, VPD) dominates vegetation responses and, more critically, how their relative influence changes over time, limiting predictions of ecosystem–climate feedback under warming. Here we analyse satellite-derived vegetation variability over the past four decades using an explainable artificial intelligence framework that disentangles nonlinear hydroclimatic driver contributions. We show SM dominates vegetation variability in most regions. However, VPD influence has strengthened while SM influence has weakened over time. These changes highlight an asymmetric transition with more SM-dominated ecosystems shifting towards increasing VPD control than vice versa. Changes in the mean and variability of SM and VPD drive this transition by altering plant water-stress responses. Continued warming will probably intensify this pattern as rising VPD and more frequent extreme events strengthen atmospheric constraints on vegetation.

title: Seismic evidence for double slab tears at the Neo-Tethyan subduction–collision transition
abstract: The transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision is a key stage in the Wilson Cycle. Yet, key processes governing this transition remain unclear owing to sparse observations of structure at depth. One such process is detachment of the subducting slab, which influences both deformation and magmatism in the overriding plate. Here we present seismic tomographic images that we interpret as evidence for two slab tears beneath southeastern Iran, where the Neo-Tethys Ocean is closing. Specifically, we show that in the Makran subduction zone, the oceanic lithosphere has continuously subducted to depths of at least 450 km, whereas in the Zagros collision zone to the west, the continental lithosphere has subducted no deeper than 300 km, resulting in east–southward slab tearing and detachment. We further identify another slab tear that probably initiated at the junction between the Makran Trench and the transform boundary and has propagated southward as the continental plate advances northward. The coexistence of these two tearing modes provides a rare snapshot of the short-lived early transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision.
